## 1. Motivation

What is the best way to learn a new skill or discipline? My old strategy was to
jump into a textbook, journal article or online course, and see where it takes
me. Sometimes it worked, but often I found myself a year later having moved on
to others things, and having forgotten almost everything I "learned."
Therefore, I've reviewed a number of books, articles, podcasts, and online
courses to see what lessons I can find. The checklist below represents my
current understanding. If you're an audio-learner and prefer podcasts,
[Tim Ferriss has an episode](https://tim.blog/2018/06/05/the-tim-ferriss-show-transcripts-the-art-and-science-of-learning-anything-faster/)
and
[Daniel Willingham has an interview](https://www.artofmanliness.com/career-wealth/career/podcast-927-beyond-lazy-learning-the-keys-to-gaining-and-retaining-knowledge/)
where many of these ideas are discussed.

## 2. How to Use this Guide

The checklist below provides a structured list of ideas for effective learning.
However,
[every person is unique](https://www.thestar.com/news/insight/2016/01/16/when-us-air-force-discovered-the-flaw-of-averages.html)
and techniques that work for 95% of the population may not work for you. I
invite you to try out anything that appeals to you; if you get the sense it's
not working, then let it go. I created a
[Google Doc template](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1eXmTy0NHVlU1x5V-xzxwAPEHgYFjMzk8KvhF7gB0R98/edit) ([PDF](../files/learning-checklist-template.pdf))
to help in applying the checklist to an area of interest for you.

## 3. Learning Checklist (A-B-C-D-E-F-G)

### Aspiration: what is your goal and why?

Clarity on the goal will help you decide where to focus and when the task is
complete.

- Are you passionate about the subject?
- Do you want to advance your career?
- Do you have a sense of wonder about the world and are following your
  curiosity?

Clarity on your intention, i.e. why this goal is important, will help you to
evaluate your progress and decide at pivotal moments whether to continue or
change course.

### Broad Overview

Getting a broad overview helps you to see how the material you might learn and
all the places you might start.

- Google searches, wikipedia pages, and YouTube videos are a great place to
  start.

### Consult Experts

Since you are trying to learn something new, your initial judgement is almost
certainly flawed. Thus it's important to get advice from others.

- Ask the experts how they learn and how they teach.
- Example questions for ultra-running and basketball are in Tim Ferriss's
  [podcast](https://tim.blog/2018/06/05/the-tim-ferriss-show-transcripts-the-art-and-science-of-learning-anything-faster/)
  and
  [book](https://www.amazon.com/Tools-Titans-Billionaires-World-Class-Performers/dp/1328683788)
  (p57).
- [Tyler Cowen has a guide](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2021/06/how-do-you-ask-good-questions.html)
  on asking good questions; he recommends Gregory Stock's
  [The Book of Questions](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B00CUMSBK2).

### Deconstruct the skill into sub-skills; then prioritize the sub-skills

Deconstruction lets you break the larger goal into smaller steps where it's
easier to make progress.

- Remember the [80/20 rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_principle) —
  that 80% of the benefits will come from learning 20% of the material.
- Identify which sub-skills to learn first. Start with either the most
  important skills, the skills that interest you most, or the easiest skills to
  learn.
- Identify which sub-skills you will not need (at least initially).
- Decide how deep into the discipline's theory you need to go. For some skills,
  a deep understanding of some underlying theory is essential (e.g.
  understanding physics) but for other skills, theory is largely unnecessary
  (e.g. driving a car).

### Establish a learning routine

A routine will help ensure you achieve your goal on time and help you learn
more efficiently.

- Consider meeting regularly with a tutor, mentor, or coach.
- Select a [Learning Approach](#sec-approaches) (see next section).
- Set a schedule:
  - Set the frequency and duration of learning sessions.
  - Ensure your dedicated learning time is focused and uninterrupted.
  - Plan breaks during your dedicated learning time to relax and allow your
    brain to make new, unplanned, connections.
- An online course may already exist that can provide a good routine for you.

### Feedback plan

Regular feedback will help you to see if you're continuing to progress toward
your goal. If progress slows, that is a good time to revisit your routine or
speak with a mentor.

- **Internal:** think about how you will regularly measure improvement and
  success.
- **External:** identify a tutor, coach or mentor to meet with regularly.

### Growth plan

Developing a long term plan for how you'll use this skill will help you to
remember the material and grow beyond the goal you had initially set for
yourself, in a way that's in line with your broader intention.

- Deepen your understanding and give back to the world by teaching the skills
  you've learned to others via a lecture, blog post, or youtube video. Creating
  a [checklist](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B086XF436Z) can help yourself and
  others effectively apply skills more effectively.

## 4. Learning Approaches {#sec-approaches}

Many approaches exist for learning a new skill. Chose the approach that works
best for you and that is appropriate for the skill. If you're overwhelmed by
the options, just pick something, try it for 10 minutes, and if you like it,
then keep going, otherwise try something else.

### Reading

- Flash research: you can learn a lot in 10 minutes, just using Google and
  Wikipedia.
- Before reading in depth, read quickly and summarize the main ideas first.
  Then, determine if you'll need to read more deeply.
- [SQ3R](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SQ3R),
  [SQ5R](https://studylib.net/doc/8451996/sq5r-study-technique), or
  [PSQ5R](https://www.indiastudychannel.com/resources/126257-PSQSR-Model-for-Reading.aspx)
  method: (Purpose), Survey, Question, Read, (Record), Recite, Review,
  (Reflect).
- How to read a journal article:
  [PDF](../files/how-to-read-a-paper.pdf) ·
  [Google Doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1jtZHKJ88PEjVr2mxWzNjG51t97CyO8rv4zoenTH_RWE/edit)

### Organizing

- [Outline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outline_%28list%29) — structured list
- [Mind map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mind_map) — structured visual
  representation
- [Checklist](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B086XF436Z) — short list of most
  important components
- [Evergreen note-taking](https://notes.andymatuschak.org/Evergreen_notes) and
  [Progressive Summarization](https://fortelabs.co/blog/progressive-summarization-a-practical-technique-for-designing-discoverable-notes/):
  create organized documents that you add to and update over time, to capture
  your developing understanding of the material.

### Teaching

- Teach the skill to a colleague.
- Write on paper how you would teach this skill to a 12 year old. Identify any
  gaps and continue learning until you can write out the idea from start to
  finish in simple language
  ([Feynman Method](https://golden.com/wiki/Feynman_Technique)).
- Give a presentation to your group.

### Doing

- Cultivate nonjudgemental awareness to see without self-criticism. Be patient
  and mindful. Then act to improve.
- Solving homework problems.
- Apply the skill to a real-life problem.
- [Katas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kata) — repeat task to gain grace and
  efficiency.

### Recalling

- Flashcards
- [Mnemonics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mnemonic)
- Drawing (e.g. for geography or anatomy)
- Writing (for vocabulary words)
- Take practice tests
- Keep glossary of new terms, and review regularly

## Useful Concepts

**Chunking.** Your mind handles masses of data by grouping it into clusters. An
example from economics is: giving → trading → selling → market → economy. Each
concept is increasingly complex and as your brain learns each one, it can then
more readily handle more complex ideas.

**Neural Pathways.** As you practice a new skill, the neural processes needed
to carry out the skill get more and more efficient, such that you're eventually
able to perform the skill without conscious thought. You can then focus your
conscious thought on learning more complex tasks.

**Making Connections.** Finding connections between what you know and what
you're learning can accelerate progress, improve recall, provide unique
insight, and make learning more fun. Josh Waitzkin does this with Chess and Tai
Chi Push-hands. I've seen this myself with Mathematical Modeling, Social
Dynamics, Individuation, and Storytelling (discussed a bit in
[Seven Basic Plots](https://www.amazon.com/Seven-Basic-Plots-Tell-Stories-ebook/dp/B00OG4EAU2))
and also with
[Music Theory and the Physics of Waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_series_%28music%29).

**[Learning Style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Learning_styles).** Know
whether your learning style is auditory, visual, reading/writing, kinesthetic,
or some combination. Use the techniques that work best for you.

## Disagreements

On my first pass through this material, I noticed some disagreement between
Josh Waitzkin and Tim Ferriss/Scott Young. I suspect it's likely that when you
get down to specifics, they'd largely agree. But for now, I just wanted to
highlight some of the disagreements, to come back to later.

**Depth vs Breadth.** Is it better to get some knowledge of a lot of concepts
in your domain, or go deep into a few?

- This probably doesn't have a simple answer, it probably depends on your
  goals.
- If you want to be the best in the world, depth in some areas will be
  essential. If you just want to be proficient, you may not need depth at all.

**Focus on the Goal vs Process.** Is it better to be driven by a goal you love,
or is it better to focus on loving the process itself?

- This also probably doesn't have a simple answer and probably depends on your
  goals.
- If you can learn what you need in 20 hours, focusing on the goal is probably
  fine.
- If it's going to take years to get to the skill level you want, it's probably
  important to find a way to love the process itself, too.
